S024.name: Depressed_Mood
S024.description: A state where a sad, empty, or hopeless mood persists.

subtypes.Depressed Mood: A persistently sunken mood or feeling of depression.
subtypes.Tearfulness: A state of frequent crying or inability to hold back tears.
subtypes.Sadness: A state where a sad or gloomy mood is maintained continuously.
subtypes.Emptiness: A feeling of inner emptiness or a state of feeling no emotion.
subtypes.Emotional Numbness: A state where emotions feel dulled or paralyzed.

S025.name: Loss_of_Interest
S025.description: A state where interest or pleasure in previously enjoyed activities is markedly diminished.

subtypes.Loss of Interest: Reduced interest in previously enjoyed hobbies or leisure activities.
subtypes.Social Withdrawal: Reduced interest or effort in social interactions and maintaining relationships.
subtypes.Loss of Motivation: Lack of motivation to initiate or complete work or tasks.
subtypes.Anhedonia: Inability to experience positive emotions such as happiness, satisfaction, love, or pleasure.
subtypes.Indifference to Achievement: Insensitivity or indifference to personal achievements or success.

S027.name: Sleep_Disturbance
S027.description: A state where there is a significant change in the quantity or quality of sleep.

subtypes.Initial Insomnia: Difficulty falling asleep and taking a long time to do so.
subtypes.Middle Insomnia: Waking up frequently during sleep or having difficulty falling back asleep.
subtypes.Early Morning Awakening: Waking up too early and being unable to fall back asleep.
subtypes.Hypersomnia: Sleeping for long periods at night or excessive sleep during the day.
subtypes.Nightmare Disorder: Sleep disturbance caused by repeated and distressing dreams.
subtypes.Non-Restorative Sleep: Feeling unrefreshed despite having slept enough.

S030.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
S030.description: Feelings of worthlessness or excessive or inappropriate guilt (which may be delusional; not merely self-reproach or guilt about being sick).

subtypes.Feelings of Worthlessness: The feeling that one is useless and has no value.
subtypes.Ruminative Guilt: A thought pattern of obsessively replaying past minor mistakes or flaws and constantly reproaching oneself.
subtypes.Excessive or Inappropriate Guilt: Feeling excessive responsibility for trivial matters or daily events and believing one deserves punishment.
subtypes.Delusional Guilt: Guilt reaching a delusional level, disconnected from reality, involving feeling responsible for unrelated unfortunate events.

S032.name: Death_Suicide
S032.description: Recurrent thoughts of death, recurrent suicidal ideation, or a suicide attempt.

subtypes.Recurrent Thoughts of Death: Passive wish to die (e.g., 'I wish I wouldn't wake up') without active intent to kill oneself.
subtypes.Suicidal Ideation: Recurring thoughts of 'I want to die' or 'I want to kill myself' without a specific plan.
subtypes.Suicidal Impulse: Strong, sudden urges to jump from a height or run into traffic without a concrete plan.
subtypes.Specific Plan for Suicide: Conceiving specific scenarios or methods regarding when, where, and how to die.
subtypes.Suicide Attempt: Actual actions taken to end one's life or preparatory behaviors like hoarding pills or writing a will.

symptom.disease_info: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is characterized by one or more episodes of at least two weeks in which there is a pervasive change in mood and/or loss of interest, accompanied by cognitive, physical, and behavioral changes that cause clinically significant distress or impairment. Typical presentations include persistent low mood, anhedonia, changes in sleep and appetite, low energy, impaired concentration, and negative cognitions such as worthlessness or suicidality, in the absence of a history of manic or hypomanic episodes. The course can be single-episode or recurrent, with episodes often triggered or unmasked by psychosocial stressors but also arising without clear external causes. Distinguishing features from related conditions (e.g., bipolar disorder, grief, adjustment disorders) include the duration and pervasiveness of symptoms, loss of reactivity of mood, and the presence of neurovegetative and cognitive changes that impair functioning across multiple domains.

patient.stressor: About eight months ago, Linh was passed over for a long-anticipated promotion to a tenure-track position in her department, despite years of positive feedback and extra work designing interdisciplinary curricula and leading workshops. The decision coincided with a heavier teaching load, a major curriculum overhaul, and pressure from colleagues to keep producing innovative course material, all while she continued late-night painting projects and community events that left her with little time to recover. Over the following months she found it increasingly difficult to keep up with grading, mentoring, and her usual creative outreach, which led to subtle criticism from a supervising professor and a sense that she was "dropping the ball" professionally. When she began canceling art activities with students, avoiding department events, and her spouse urged her to talk to someone after noticing how withdrawn she had become from work she used to love, she agreed to seek psychiatric evaluation.
patient.chief_complaint: I don’t enjoy my classes or my art anymore, and the things that used to excite me just feel flat and pointless.

patient.stressor: Around eight months ago, Ruben’s adult daughter moved out of state after a serious argument about his long work hours and missed family events, leaving their relationship strained and contact minimal. This happened on the heels of increasing tension at home about his frequent evening client meetings and travel, which had long been a source of pride for him as the family provider. As time passed without reconciliation, he began pulling back from extended family gatherings he once hosted, stopped planning his usual trips to Mexico, and his performance at work slipped enough that his manager questioned whether he still had the "fire" for sales. When he recently confided to a cousin during a family fiesta that he felt like he had "failed as a father" and admitted to thinking his family might be better off without him, his cousin and wife insisted he see a mental health professional, leading to the current consultation.
patient.chief_complaint: I can’t shake this feeling that I’ve failed my family and that everything that’s gone wrong is my fault.

patient.stressor: Roughly eight months ago, Shalini’s older sister in California was diagnosed with a chronic cardiac condition, and Shalini gradually took on a long-distance caregiving role—coordinating appointments, managing finances, and making frequent trips while trying to maintain her mentoring and community art circle in Corvallis. The ongoing responsibility, combined with her own aging-related fatigue and living alone as a divorced woman, led her to cut back on watercolor groups, walking clubs, and social dinners that had previously structured her weeks. Over time, friends noticed she was canceling plans more often, falling behind on organizing her intergenerational art-and-learning circle, and seeming preoccupied and emotionally withdrawn, despite insisting she was "just tired." When her primary care physician saw a marked change from her usually engaged, organized self during a routine check-up and heard how long this had been going on, he recommended a psychiatric evaluation, which she accepted after realizing she no longer felt like herself day to day.
patient.chief_complaint: For months now I’ve had this constant heavy, sad feeling that I just can’t seem to shake, even when I’m doing things I used to enjoy.
